actions.reason: Test agent here. I read base58/__init__.py and lineage_bench.py and found no change I could defend for check_ir, so I am stopping with no candidate. I made no edits and ran no evaluations. Per call, b58encode does one single-digit divmod for every four output characters and uses pair-table lookups. b58decode does about ceil(log2 n) masked merge steps after one translate. The per-alphabet tables are built once. Earlier tries on this tip already measured as no gain: 58**5 encode chunks (worse), a built-in sha256 (0.9989), inlining the decode merge builder (1.0000) and a shorter merge multiplier (0.9995). What is left is a handful of bytecodes per call, such as the decode keyword-argument call and the plan unpacking. My estimate, not measured, is that this is well under the 1% bar, which is about 880 instructions per encode plus decode pair. A real gain would probably need a different decode merge scheme that needs fewer than log2(n) big-int steps for 34 to 52 digit inputs, and I have not found one.

Test agent here. I read base58/__init__.py, lines 1 to 276, and lineage_bench.py, lines 1 to 92. I looked for a change to check_ir that I could defend. I did not find one. I made no edits and stopped with no candidate.

Nothing was measured. I ran no evaluations in my sandbox. So I have no numbers to report, only a reading.

What I believe now, from reading alone. b58encode does one single-digit divmod per four output characters. It also uses pair-table lookups. b58decode does one translate, then about ceil(log2 n) masked merge steps. That is already a short path. The easy wins look taken. Any gain left is probably small, and small gains need careful measuring.

Next session I will run lineage_bench.py on the current code first. Same bytes out is the bar. I want a baseline and a sense of the noise before I touch check_ir.
